sec.title: Background
sec.p: Olaparib, a poly ADP-ribose polymerase inhibitor, was approved by the European Commission in December 2022 and for which the Health for technology Assessment (HtA body) issued a favorable opinion for reimbursement in France on 5 April, 2023, following the results of the PROpel phase III clinical trial, for the first-line treatment of metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer in combination with abiraterone and prednisone or prednisolone in adult men for whom chemotherapy is not clinically indicated.

sec.title: Objective
sec.p: This publication aimed to report the first real-world data of patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer who received a combination of first-line olaparib with abiraterone, plus prednisone or prednisolone in the funded Early Access (fEA) for olaparib in France, from 30 March, 2023, to 25 September, 2024.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Eligible patients were adult men with first-line metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer. Olaparib 300-mg twice-daily tablets was given in combination with abiraterone plus prednisone or prednisolone regardless of the homologous recombination repair gene mutation status. Characteristics of the population, treatment duration, reasons for discontinuation, and safety data were collected during the fEA period. Patients could continue to receive olaparib after the end of the fEA.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: A total of 84 physicians spread over 72 hospitals in metropolitan France requested a fEA for 176 patients, 154 (87.5%) of whom were eligible to be included in the early access program. In total, 118 (76.6%) patients had an unknown homologous recombination repair status. Half of the patients (76, 49.7%) had very aggressive cancer with a Gleason score of 8 while 11 (7.2%) of them had a low-grade cancer with a Gleason score of 6 at the diagnosis. The most common metastatic sites were bone (107 patients, 69.5%) and distant (60, 39.0%) or regional (42, 27.3%) lymph nodes. Among the 154 patients, 84 (54.5%) had medical history, 47 (56.0%) of whom had arterial hypertension. All included patients had received at least one prior treatment prior to the metastatic castration resistance stage. Most patients (145, 94.2%) had received androgen suppression and 70 (45.5%) had been treated with androgen receptor pathway inhibitors. Of the 154 patients, 153 (99.4%) had at least one concomitant treatment with abiraterone and prednisone or prednisolone. Data confirming administration of olaparib treatment were provided for 149 patients (exposed patients), of whom 140 (94.0%) received olaparib at initiation at the dose of 300 mg twice daily. Fifty-seven patients experienced a total of 60 adverse events (36 serious adverse events and 24 non-serious adverse events). Over this period, three fatal and five life-threatening events were reported. The three fatal adverse events were one death assessed as a suspected adverse reaction (pancytopenia) and two deaths assessed as unrelated to olaparib: one attributed to disease progression and one to suicide. Because of adverse events, dose reductions were made in five patients, treatment was temporarily interrupted in one patient and discontinued in 20 patients.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: These are the first results describing the real-world use of olaparib in France in prostate cancer. Most patients included in the fEA had generally similar characteristics as the patients randomized in the PROpel clinical trial (NCT03732820) and initiated at the standard dose of 300 mg twice daily. No new safety signals were reported in this real-world patient population. The analyzed data did not modify the benefit-risk balance of olaparib.

tr.td: In France, the regulatory procedure for funded Early Access allows rapid and fair access to investigational drugs, bringing life-changing treatments to patients as early as possible.

The data generated by this funded Early Access correlate with the previously demonstrated clinical safety profile from the pivotal trial of olaparib in combination with abiraterone as a first-line treatment for metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer, representing a significant advancement in metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer treatment.

These “real-world” data of olaparib highlighted the use of the combination strategy in patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer with unmutated/unknown homologous recombination repair status and also pretreated with androgen receptor pathway inhibitors.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Prostate cancer is the leading cancer in men in France with an incidence of 59,885 cases/year in France in 2018 and represents 24% of all male incident cancers. The median age at diagnosis is 64 years [1, 2]. After a clear decline in incidence between 2005 and 2012, prostate cancer has shown a significant changing trend with a new increasing incidence since 2015 [3]. Prostate cancer ranks third among cancer deaths in men in France (9200 deaths estimated in 2021) [1]. It is a cancer with a very good prognosis with a 5-year survival rate of 93% for men diagnosed between 2010 and 2015, although 80% of cancers are diagnosed at a localized stage [1]. However, approximately 10–20% of men with advanced prostate cancer will develop castration-resistant prostate cancer within 5 years, and at least 84% of these men will have metastases at the time of castration-resistant prostate cancer diagnosis [4]. Of patients with no metastases at castration-resistant prostate cancer diagnosis, 33% are likely to develop metastases within 2 years [4]. Despite improved care, metastatic prostate cancer accounts for 50% of mortality from this cancer, and the 5-year survival rate for these metastatic patients is only 28% [5]. Patients in first-line metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) clinical trials have a median overall survival of approximately 3 years. In real-world clinical practice, median overall survival is less than 2 years. Approximately half of the patients do not progress to a second line of life-prolonging systemic therapy, emphasizing the need to maximize results with first-line treatment in mCRPC [6]. Recently, there has been an increase in drug approvals in the advanced prostate cancer field. In the past, the androgen receptor (AR) was not considered a relevant target in the development of castration resistance, but it has now emerged as a valid therapeutic target, leading to a redefinition of terms such as ‘hormone resistance’ to ‘castration resistance’ [7]. According to the French recommendations of ccAFU (French Urology Association Cancer Committee) [8], the therapeutic strategy in mCRPC relies on alternating either androgen receptor pathway inhibitors (ARPIs) [abiraterone acetate, enzalutamide, darolutamide, and apalutamide] or taxane-based chemotherapy. However, there is a significant need to improve the understanding and management of this disease, in particular, to avoid progression to conditions with high mortality rates and to assess patients outside of a clinical trial setting [9]. Genomic profiling studies have uncovered significant genomic heterogeneity across distinct stages of prostate cancer. Pritchard et al. found germline DNA damage response mutations in 4.6% of localized prostate cancer cases, increasing to 11.8% in men with mCRPC [10]. Disruptions in homologous recombination repair (HRR) pathways create vulnerabilities that can be exploited by poly(ADP‑ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors via synthetic lethality [11]. Additionally, advances in molecular characterization have emphasized the crucial role of HRR genes alterations in cancer development and progression, supporting PARP inhibition as an attractive therapeutic strategy [12]. Preclinical investigations have demonstrated a crosstalk between AR signaling pathways and DNA damage response genes, indicating a potential induction of BRCAness and supporting the exploration of synthetic lethality through combined AR signaling and PARP inhibition. Recent clinical trials have shown promising responses to such combination therapies, even in patients with mCRPC without specific DNA damage response gene alterations [13, 14]. Olaparib, a PARP inhibitor, has received approval as monotherapy for the treatment of specific patient populations with ovarian, breast, pancreatic, and most recently, prostate cancer.

Building on its established use across multiple cancer types, including prostate cancer, the PROpel (NCT03732820) study, a randomized, double-blind, phase III trial, investigated the efficacy of first-line olaparib in combination with abiraterone versus placebo plus abiraterone in patients with mCRPC, irrespective of HRR gene mutation (HRRm) status. PROpel successfully met its primary endpoint, demonstrating a statistically significant and clinically meaningful radiographic progression-free survival (rPFS) benefit with olaparib plus abiraterone compared with abiraterone plus placebo (24.8 vs 16.6 months; hazard ratio, 0.66; 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.54–0.81; p <0.001) [15]. These positive results led to the European approval of olaparib plus abiraterone and prednisone/prednisolone in December 2022 for patients with mCRPC for whom chemotherapy is not clinically indicated. Because of these positive results, on 30 March, 2023, the Health for technology Assessment (HtA body) granted early access to olaparib for the indication “in combination with abiraterone and prednisone or prednisolone for the treatment of adult patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer for whom chemotherapy is not clinically indicated.”

This program aims to simplify and fast track access to innovative medications, particularly those used in rare, severe, or disabling diseases where no alternatives exist. Its primary objective is to promptly assess the effectiveness of expected benefits through the collection and analysis of real-world data, ultimately enhancing patient care and safety for individuals in therapeutic impasses or unable to wait for conventional medication availability or clinical trial participation. The program applies to innovative medications, authorizing and funding them in the early stages of their development (pre-authorization) or while awaiting reimbursement approval (post-authorization), until they are fully integrated into the standard authorization and reimbursement framework for healthcare products. In this context, this article reports a summary of this post-authorization funded Early Access (fEA) of olaparib over the period from 30 March, 2023, to 25 September, 2024, for adult patients with mCRPC in the first line, regardless of the HRRm status.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: “Early access” is a mechanism that allows patients with no therapeutic options to receive, on an exceptional and temporary basis, certain medicines that are not authorized or reimbursed yet for a specific therapeutic indication. Early access has been revised and put in place in July 2021 following PLFSS 2021. All five of the following conditions must be met to have an early access:

list-item.p: The benefit/risk ratio is presumed favorable.
The medicine is intended to treat serious, rare, or disabling diseases.
The medicine is considered innovative, notably with regard to any clinically relevant comparator.

sec.p: Early access applies:

list-item.p: To medicines that have a marketing authorization (MA) for the indication in question but have not yet been approved for reimbursement by the national health insurance.

To medicines that do not have an MA for the indication in question and for which the company commits to submitting an application. In this case, the French National Agency for Medicines and Health Products Safety (ANSM) must issue a favorable opinion on efficacy and safety based on clinical trial results before the HtA body makes its decision. The patient’s data collection is formalized through the therapeutic use and data collection protocol (PUT-RD), which is a legal protocol required for each early access request and describes methods of collecting patient data. All patient data collected are pseudonymized to respect the Declaration of Helsinki. The PROpel early access database is the dedicated repository that houses all patient-level data collected under the fEA program, including eligibility, baseline characteristics, treatment exposure, and safety events for patients enrolled in early access.

sec.p: The HtA body granted on 30 March, 2023 an early access authorization following MA for olaparib 100 and 150 mg “in combination with abiraterone and prednisone or prednisolone for the treatment of adult patients with metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) for whom chemotherapy is not clinically indicated.” The provision of the medicine under this early access authorization began on 25 April, 2023. This medicine received an MA in France on 16 December, 2022 for the same indication as the early access: olaparib is indicated in combination with abiraterone and prednisone or prednisolone for the treatment of adult patients with mCRPC for whom chemotherapy is not clinically indicated.

The early access authorization was renewed on 2 April, 2024 and ended on 25 September, 2024 following the publication in the Official Journal (JORF) registering the specialty olaparib on the list of reimbursable pharmaceutical specialties. Eligibility criteria of the early access authorization program for olaparib include the following:

list-item.p: Participants must be aged 18 years or older.
The patient must have mCRPC that is no longer responding to androgen deprivation therapy.

Participants should be candidates for treatment with abiraterone, prednisone, or prednisolone, and must exhibit documented disease progression as defined by one or more of the following criteria while on androgen deprivation therapy:
Demonstrated by at least two increases in prostate specific antigen levels, with a minimum interval of 1 week between each measurement. The prostate specific antigen value must be ≥1 μg/L (1 ng/mL), adhering to Prostate Cancer Working Group 3 criteria.
Characterized by the appearance of two or more new lesions on a bone scan, according to Prostate Cancer Working Group 3 criteria.
Blood testosterone level must be ≤50 ng/dL (≤2.0 nmol/L) within the prior 28 days.
Chemotherapy should not be clinically indicated at this time.
Patients must not have received prior treatment for mCRPC.

sec.p: Regarding data collection, inclusions covered the period from 30 March 2023 to 25 September, 2024, the date of publication in the Official Journal. However, data collection continued until 25 October, 2024, to increase the return of termination forms, and the database was frozen on that same date. Data were collected from treatment access request forms completed by physicians for this fEA of olaparib. Physicians also reported adverse events (AEs) to their regional pharmacovigilance centers (CRPV) or AstraZeneca.

The request forms captured information on the diagnosis, patient condition, comorbidities, prior treatments at the metastatic castration stage, as well as concomitant treatments and supportive care. Discontinuation of olaparib may occur because of AEs, defined as any untoward medical occurrence, including adverse drug reactions and serious adverse drug reactions, and must be reported on end-of-treatment forms.

The dosage of olaparib was 300 mg (two 150-mg tablets) taken twice daily, orally, for a total daily dose of 600 mg. A 100-mg tablet was available for dose reduction. Treatment was recommended to continue until progression of the underlying disease or until unacceptable toxicity. Analyses were performed on the included patients for whom an early access authorization was requested and accepted. Data collection of the fEA will be discontinued upon the determination of pricing and reimbursement in France but continuity of treatment will be ensured outside of fEA. The holder of the PROpel early access database is AstraZeneca. Figure 1 shows the main patient flows in the early access analysis to clarify which subset was used for each analysis.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: From 30 March, 2023 (date of fEA approval) to 25 September, 2024, 176 adult men were the subject of a treatment access request by olaparib in the context of the fEA. Among them, 154 patients (87.5%) were eligible and were included in the fEA. However, 22 patients were denied access because they did not meet all the eligibility criteria: 19 patients were not in the first line of mCRPC, one patient was not at the mCRPC stage, one patient was not progressive at the time of the request, and one patient was on monotherapy and not in combination with prednisone and abiraterone (Fig. 1).

sec.title: Requesters
sec.p: In total, 84 physicians across 72 hospitals in metropolitan France requested participation in the fEA. Most of these physicians were oncology specialists (81 physicians, 96.4%), and three were reported as “competent in cancerology.” Among the 72 hospitals, 29 (40.3%) were general hospitals (CHG), 25 (34.7%) were private centers, 8 (11.1%) were comprehensive cancer centers, and 10 (13.9%) were university hospitals (CHU). The median number of patients included per hospital was one, with a range from 1 to 15 patients, with a similar distribution among prescribers. Figure 2 presents the geographical distribution of requesting physicians and included patients by region.

sec.title: Patient Characteristics
sec.p: The patients who had access to the fEA had a median age of 75.9 years (range 46.9–91.8 years), the median time between the initial diagnosis of prostate cancer and the request for early access to treatment was 57.4 months (range 3.3–324.8 months). A total of 91 (59.5%) patients had localized or locally advanced prostate cancer and 10 (6.5%) had mCRPC at initial diagnosis of the disease. All patients included in the fEA had metastatic disease. The median time between the diagnosis of metastases and the request for treatment access was 23.6 months (range 0.1–126.0 months), the most common metastatic sites were bone (69.5%) and distant (39%) or regional (27.3%) lymph nodes. It should be noted that patients could have several metastatic sites. The median time between the diagnosis of mCRPC and the request for treatment access was 1.4 months (range 0.0–114.6 months). The patients had mostly an unknown HRR status (76.6%) while 13 (8.4%) of them harbored HRRm, 23 (14.9%) harbored non-HRRm. Most patients were in good general condition, with Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group (ECOG) scores of 0 (55.2%) or 1 (39.6%). Half of the patients (49.7%) had very aggressive cancer with a Gleason score of 8 while 23.5% of patients had a Gleason score of 7 (3+4) and 19.6% of them had a score of 7 (4+3). A minority of patients (7.2%) had a low-grade cancer with a Gleason score of 6 at diagnosis. The median value of the last prostate specific antigen dosage at the time of the treatment access was 6.0 µg/L (range 0.0–240.0 µg/L). The blood pressure at the time of the treatment access request was also collected and 41.6% of patients had associated arterial hypertension (Table 1).

sec.title: Comorbidities and Previous Treatments
sec.p: Regarding comorbidities, among the 154 patients included in the fEA, 84 (54.5%) had a medical history of interest, 47 of whom (56%) had arterial hypertension (treated or not), sometimes associated with other comorbidities. Among the 154 patients included, 7 (4.5%) had a history of other cancer in the past 5 years (including a cutaneous carcinoma of the face and a non-muscle invasive bladder cancer). Most patients (95.5%) did not have a history of other cancer in the previous 5 years (Table 2 and Table S2 of the Electronic Supplementary Material [ESM]).

sec.p: A minority of patients (13 out of 154, or 8.4%) had a history of venous thromboembolic events, such as cerebellar stroke, pulmonary embolism, and recurrent deep vein thrombosis associated with paroxysmal atrial fibrillation (complete arrhythmia due to atrial fibrillation). However, most patients (91.6%) had no such history.

All patients who received early access treatment had received at least one prior treatment before reaching the metastatic castration resistance stage. Most patients (145, 94.2%) had received androgen suppression. Nearly half of these patients (70, 45.5%) were pretreated with an ARPI (one patient had been treated with several ARPIs): 26 patients (37.1%) enzalutamide, 25 patients (35.7%) abiraterone, 15 patients (21.4%) apalutamide, and 5 patients (7.1%) darolutamide. A minority of patients (11, 7.1%) had received docetaxel (Table 2).

sec.title: Treatment Modalities with Olaparib
sec.p: Within the context of the fEA, olaparib had to be used “in combination with abiraterone and prednisone or prednisolone.” This criterion was met as 100% of the patients had at least one concomitant treatment with abiraterone and prednisone or prednisolone. In addition, some patients (16 patients or 10.4%) were also receiving palliative radiotherapy, and 40 patients (26%) were receiving anti-resorptive agents (38 of them denosumab, one of them zoledronic acid, and one patient had received vitamin D [cholecalciferol]).

Among the 154 patients included in the early access program, 149 were exposed to olaparib. Notably, in five cases, physicians reported that olaparib was ultimately not initiated, and data were missing for one patient. Overall, data were available for 148 of the 149 patients exposed.

Regarding treatment modalities, most patients (140, 94.0%) initiated olaparib at the standard Summary of Product Characteristics (SmPC) dose of 300 mg twice daily. In nine patients (6.0%), the dosage was reduced to 200 mg twice daily, as recommended for patients with renal insufficiency. The time between the treatment access request and the planned date of initiation was relatively short, with a median time of 7 days (range −7 to 83 days) [Table 3]. Note that this negative delay corresponded to a patient who initiated treatment before inclusion in the fEA. It should be noted that six patients initiated olaparib treatment prior to enrollment in the early access program. This primarily resulted from physician errors, whereby treatment was prescribed through the standard pathway and the situation was subsequently regularized by enrolling the patients in the early access program after a median duration of 4.3 months (minimum 0.2 months; maximum 8.0 months).

sec.title: Pretreatment with Androgen Receptor Pathway Inhibitors (ARPIs)
sec.p: In this fEA, 70 (45.5%) patients with a median age of 76 years (range 60–92 years) were pretreated with ARPIs (Table 4). At the time of access request, 34 patients (49.3%) had a Gleason score of 8 or higher and an International Society of Urological Pathology grade of 4 or higher. Among these 70 patients, 40 (57.1%) had a significant medical history (Table S4 of the ESM), of whom 26 (65%) had arterial hypertension, and seven patients (10%) had thromboembolic events as part of their medical background. Only 2 out of the 70 patients required a dose reduction by 200 mg twice daily (two 100-mg tablets) for renal failure (1onepatient) and dizziness, digestive problems, and costal pain (one patient) [Table 4].

sec.p: Among the 70 patients pre-treated with ARPIs, nine completed a treatment discontinuation form, after a median time between the request for access to treatment and discontinuation of 2.8 months (range 1.4–7.8 months). At treatment discontinuation, two (22.2%) out of these nine patients were receiving a dose reduction. The reasons for discontinuation of olaparib were suspected adverse drug reactions in two (22.2%) patients, disease progression in six (66.7%), unsatisfactory therapeutic effect in one (11.1%), patient choice in one (11.1%), and death in another one (11.1%). The cause of death was suicide that occurred 2.9 months after the request for access. Further treatment was initiated in four of the nine patients who discontinued olaparib with chemotherapy in three patients that included docetaxel in two patients and cabazitaxel in another one patient, or an ARPI with abiraterone in one patient (Table 4).

sec.title: Safety and Tolerability
sec.p: Safety analyses were conducted among patients who received at least one dose of olaparib (treated cohort: n = 148, consistent with Sect. 3.5). Adverse events reported in patients who never initiated olaparib were excluded from the safety analysis. Percentages are calculated using the treated cohort as the denominator; see Table 5. During the fEA period and follow-up from 30 March, 2023, to 25 October, 2024, 57 (38.5%) patients experienced a total of 60 AEs (36 serious AEs and 24 non-serious AEs) [Table 5]. Over this period, three (2.0%) fatal and five (3.4%) life-threatening events were reported. The three fatal AEs were one death assessed as a suspected adverse reaction (pancytopenia) and two deaths assessed as unrelated to olaparib: one attributed to disease progression and one to suicide. The life-threatening events were considered as AEs including anemia in one patient and atrial fibrillation, cardiac failure, hepatic ischemia, and intestinal ischemia in another patient. In six (4.1%) patients, the dose was reduced because of AEs (headache, asthenia (3), renal impairment, abdominal pain, dyspnea, abnormal general physical condition, gastrointestinal disorders, fatigue, nausea). In one (0.7%) patient, there was a temporary interruption because of an AE of anemia. In 20 (13.5%) patients, treatment was discontinued because of AEs (anemia (7), neutropenia, pancytopenia, thrombocytopenia (3), atrial fibrillation, cardiac failure, diarrhea, intestinal ischemia, unspecified AEs (6), asthenia (3), drug intolerance, fatigue (2), deterioration of general physical health, pain, pyrexia, hepatic ischemia, urinary tract infection, decreased glomerular filtration rate, abnormal neutrophil count, decreased appetite, renal failure (2), renal impairment, dyspnea and lung disorder). No new safety signals were identified in the reported cases throughout the entire duration of the early access program, and the benefit-risk balance of olaparib remains unchanged [16]. The data collected as part of the early access program do not alter the benefit-risk balance of olaparib or the known safety profile described in the SmPC.

sec.title: End of Treatment
sec.p: Throughout the total period of the early access program, 30 patients permanently discontinued treatment. For five of them, physicians indicated that the patient ultimately never initiated treatment with olaparib. For the remaining 25 patients, discontinuation occurred after short durations of exposure to olaparib (median 3.4 months [minimum 1.4 months to maximum 8.0 months]) [Table 6] [16].

sec.p: Among the 25 patients, the reasons for discontinuation of olaparib treatment were the occurrence of suspected treatment-related AEs in 12 (48%) patients, with olaparib suspected adverse drug reactions in ten (83.3%) of them, disease progression in eight (32%), discontinuation because of an unsatisfactory therapeutic effect in two patients (8%), death in three (12%), patient’s choice in four (16%), and diagnosis of concomitant gastric adenocarcinoma in another one (4%).
A total of three patients (12%) died. The cause of death reported was AE in one patient (33.3%), disease progression in one (33.3%), and suicide in another one (33.3%) [Table 6].

Among the 25 patients, five (20%) were receiving a dose reduction by 200 mg twice daily (two 100-mg tablets) and another two (8%) participants required another dose that was 250 mg twice daily (one patient) or 300 mg daily (one patient). The reasons for dose reduction were provided for four of the five patients in the patient’s form (one patient data missing) and included renal failure (one patient), dizziness, digestive problems and costal pain (one patient), grade 2 asthenia (one patient), and renal failure followed by persistent grade 3 anemia after management of the AE (one patient).

Initiation of further treatment after discontinuation of olaparib was reported for 11 of 25 patients. Of the 11 patients, 5 (45.5%) were treated with chemotherapy including docetaxel in four, cabazitaxel in one, four (36.4%) were treated with ARPIs including abiraterone in two, enzalutamide in one, decapeptyl, abiraterone, prednisone in another one, one (9.1%) was treated with pembrolizumab, and one (9.1%) reported no further treatment (Table 6).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: In France, the regulatory procedure for fEA allows rapid and fair access to drugs on the presumption of efficacy and safety, bringing innovative treatments to patients as early as possible. This authorization is granted on an exceptional basis and for a period of 1 year. However, if early access provides data confirming or refuting the clinical benefit of the drugs, the HtA body is authorized to renew or suspend early access.

Additionally, this type of program could generate “real-world data” referring to information on the use and outcomes of specific new treatments and technologies under conditions of real-life clinical practice [17] while randomized clinical trials include suitable patients with no comorbidities. Real-world data reflect the safety and effectiveness of treatments from clinical practice in a real-world setting and thereby provide an assessment of benefits to the population treated outside of clinical trials [18]. Valuable additional information for physicians, patients, and policy makers is provided through an understanding of the outcomes in the real-world population treated. However, given that the PUT-RD does not include follow-up forms and considering the small number of discontinuation forms received, it is not possible to draw conclusions regarding treatment efficacy in this specific fEA.

Over the period from 30 March, 2023, to 25 September, 2024, 154 requests have been approved. In total, 149 patients with mCRPC have been exposed and benefited from olaparib. Patients included were older than those in the PROpel population with a mean age of 75.9 years (range 46.9–91.8 years) versus 69 years (range 43–91 years) in PROpel. Collected data at the time of inclusion in the fEA describe the severity of the disease at the start of treatment with olaparib. Most patients were in good general condition, with ECOG scores of 0 (55.2%) or 1 (39.6%) similar to those reported in the PROpel trial [ECOG 0 (71.7%); ECOG 1 (28.1%)]. A total of 66.4% of patients in PROpel had very aggressive cancer with a Gleason score ≥8 versus 49.7% in fEA. Most patients in the cohort had metastases in bones (69.5%), distant lymph nodes (39%), or locoregional lymph nodes (27.3%), which is comparable to the population in the PROpel phase III clinical trial [bones (87.5%) and distant (33.3%) or regional (20.6%) lymph nodes] [15]. Regarding comorbidities, 84 patients (54.5%) had a relevant medical history. A reclassification of these data identified that 47 of these 84 patients (56%) had arterial hypertension (treated or untreated), sometimes associated with other comorbidities. This represents a major difference from the PROpel trial, which excluded patients with uncontrolled hypertension [15].

Olaparib in combination with abiraterone and prednisone or prednisolone reduced the risk of disease progression or death by 34.0% versus abiraterone and prednisone or prednisolone, the standard of care treatment in the PROpel trial (based on a hazard ratio of 0.66; 95% CI 0.54–0.81; p < 0.0001). The median rPFS was 24.8 months for olaparib plus abiraterone versus 16.6 months for abiraterone alone. Furthermore, a planned rPFS analysis by blinded independent central review showed olaparib plus abiraterone had a median rPFS of 27.6 months compared with 16.4 months with abiraterone alone, extending median rPFS by almost 1 year [15]. In addition, the median overall survival was 42.1 months (95% CI 38.4–not reached) with olaparib plus abiraterone and 34.7 months (31.0–39.3) with placebo plus abiraterone (hazard ratio of 0.81, 95% CI 0.67–1.00; p = 0.054) [19].

In PROpel, olaparib is combined with abiraterone, an ARPI that targets the AR pathway. Androgen receptor signaling engages a transcriptional program that is critical for tumor cell growth and survival in prostate cancer [20, 21]. Preclinical models have identified interactions between PARP signaling and the AR pathway that support the observation of a combined anti-tumor effect of olaparib and ARPIs, like abiraterone, in both HRR-deficient and HRR-proficient prostate cancer [22–24]. The PARP1 protein has been reported to be required for the transcriptional activity of ARs; therefore, inhibiting PARP with olaparib may impair the expression of AR target genes and enhance the activity of ARPIs [20, 23, 25]. Additionally, it is thought that abiraterone may alter the transcription of some HRR genes, which may induce the HRR-deficient phenotype, which may increase sensitivity to PARP inhibition [22, 24, 26, 27].

The data collected as part of the fEA in a real-world setting did not modify the benefit-risk balance of olaparib. No pharmacovigilance signal was identified from the cases reported during the entire period covered by the PROpel early access final report. [16].

The safety and tolerability profile of olaparib in combination with abiraterone in the fEA was in line with that observed in prior clinical trials and the known safety profiles of the individual drugs. Consistent with PROpel, the most frequently observed adverse drug reactions in this EA cohort were hematologic toxicities (notably anemia and other cytopenias) and asthenia/fatigue, with no unexpected toxicity patterns [15, 19]. The absence of any increased or unexpected risk is corroborated by national pharmacovigilance during the PROpel early access as documented in the final summary, which identified no new safety signals [16].

Moreover, the conditions of use of olaparib in the fEA were those set out in the PUT-RD, with most patients initiating at the standard dose of 600 mg/day (94%), while a minority of patients for whom the dose had to be adapted (such as for patients with renal insufficiency or anemia) initiated at the reduced dose of 400 mg/day as indicated in the SmPC. Similarly, all patients were treated in combination with abiraterone and prednisone or prednisolone.

Unlike the PROpel study, which did not include patients pretreated with ARPIs, this early access program demonstrates that 70 (45.5%) out of 154 patients received olaparib and were pretreated with ARPIs. This also represents a major difference from the phase III PROpel clinical trial, which did not include patients with prior exposure to second-generation hormone therapy. No signals of inefficacy were observed in this subgroup, with only 9 out of 70 patients discontinuing treatment during the access period. This real-world use of olaparib aligns with the latest recommendations from the French Association of Urology, advocating for the first-line use of PARP inhibitors in patients pretreated with ARPIs.

In conclusion, no discrepancy was observed between the population included in the early access and the eligibility criteria specified in the PUT-RD. Patients included in the early access had characteristics broadly similar to those of patients randomized in the PROpel study [15, 19]. The early access made it possible to include a broader population reflecting real-world practice, notably including patients with hypertension, patients previously treated with second-generation hormone therapy, and a large proportion of patients with unknown HRR status, which was not the case in the PROpel trial. Treatments administered prior to olaparib were consistent with clinical practice and current recommendations for metastatic hormone-sensitive patients. This early access analysis has limitations as it remains descriptive, relies on data reported by physicians, and draws no conclusions regarding treatment efficacy. Nevertheless, given the low rates of missing data, with a range from 0 to 4.5% depending on the parameters, this study was conducted in a comprehensive manner. Furthermore, these data represent the first real-world evidence on the use of olaparib in this indication across France, pending the larger-scale results from the PROWESs (NCT03732820) and PROceed (NCT06380738) studies. Our real-world study also provides valuable information on the combination of olaparib plus abiraterone therapy for physicians, patients and policy makers to further improve the outcomes of patients with prostate cancer.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer represents a significant therapeutic challenge and the prognosis for these patients remains poor. Given the fatal nature of mCRPC and the increasing difficulty in managing disease progression, it is essential to continue improving therapeutic strategies from the first line of treatment. Olaparib is the first PARP inhibitor approved in December 2022 as combination drug for the first-line treatment of mCRPC. This approval is based on the results of the phase III PROpel trial that demonstrated olaparib plus abiraterone reduce the risk of disease progression or death by 34.0%.

In 18 months, 154 patients, 45.5% of whom pretreated with ARPIs, were enrolled in the fEA program highlighting the strong unmet need for patients with mCRPC in first-line treatment. No new safety signals were identified during the fEA. The data collected within the framework of the early access program did not modify the established benefit-risk profile of olaparib or its known safety profile as described in the SmPC. The MA holder for olaparib continues active surveillance of this medicine. The results of safety in this early access program confirm the results demonstrated in the phase III clinical trial PROpel and support the MA granted to olaparib in December 2022 “in combination with abiraterone and prednisone or prednisolone for the treatment of adult patients with mCRPC for whom chemotherapy is not clinically indicated.” Therefore, the combination of olaparib with abiraterone represents a significant advancement in mCRPC treatment.

sec.title: Ethical Approval
sec.p: Early access authorizations are granted by the HtA body since 1 July, 2021 for innovative medicines following an opinion from the ANSM as to their presumed efficacy and safety ratio. Ten months after this reform came into force through the 2021 French social security financing law, the HtA body and the ANSM issued a positive initial report on this procedure, which fast tracks and facilitates patient access to innovative medicines. This study followed the ethical principles set out in the Declaration of Helsinki. The process is formalized through the therapeutic use and data collection protocol (PUT-RD), which is a legal dossier required for each early access request and describes the methods of collecting patient data. All patient data collected are pseudonymized to respect the Declaration of Helsinki.

sec.title: Consent to Participate
sec.p: The patients did receive a patient information leaflet from their physician. Patient consent was collected by the physician prior to administration of the medicine. This was mandatory and applied to all patients included in this study.
